title: Channels, select and pipelines
goal: By the end you can pick a channel capacity, build a fan-out and fan-in worker pipeline with produce, race calls with select, bridge a listener API with callbackFlow, and choose between buffer, conflate and collectLatest.

warmup.q: Three worker coroutines each run `for (id in ids) settle(id)` over the same `Channel<String>`, and a producer sends 9 ids into it, then closes it. How many times is each id settled?
options: Three times: every worker gets every id
Exactly once: each element goes to one receiver
Once, but all 9 go to whichever worker started first
It can't work: only one coroutine may receive from a channel
warmup.why: A channel is a queue: each element is received by exactly one receiver. Several receivers on one channel is fan-out, and the channel serves waiting receivers fairly, so the ids spread across the three workers. Delivering every value to every subscriber is what a SharedFlow does.

code.title: FlowBackpressure.kt

alt.title: FlowBackpressureJava.java

try.expect: Plain: `1 2 3` in about 1,200 ms. `buffer()`: `1 2 3` in about 1,000 ms. `conflate()`: `1 3` in about 700 ms. `collectLatest`: `start 1, start 2, start 3, done 3` in about 600 ms. With a 50 ms collector, `conflate()` prints `1 2 3`: it only skips values that arrive while the collector is busy, and now it never is. The Java twin prints the same values in about the same times with `concatMap`, `onBackpressureBuffer`, `onBackpressureLatest` and `switchMap`.

analogy: A channel is the hatch between a restaurant's kitchen and its dining room. With a rendezvous hatch there is no shelf: the cook holds the plate until a waiter takes it. A buffered hatch has a shelf with a fixed number of spots, and the cook waits only when the shelf is full. Fan-out is several waiters taking plates from the same hatch, each plate going to exactly one of them. Fan-in is several cooks passing plates through one hatch to one waiter. `select` is ringing two suppliers and going with whoever picks up first, then hanging up on the other. The analogy breaks at closing time: in a real kitchen the staff see the lights go off. A channel's receivers only learn that nothing more is coming when someone calls `close()`, and if nobody does, they wait at the hatch forever.
in_your_world: A worker pool over a channel is a good fit for settlement and refund batches: size the pool to what the acquirer allows (say, 8 concurrent calls), and the channel keeps everything else waiting without holding a thread. Rendezvous or small buffers keep memory flat when the acquirer slows down. `select` with `onAwait` and `onTimeout` is the shape of a hedged authorization or a fallback acquirer: take the first answer within 800 ms, otherwise route elsewhere, and cancel what you no longer need. `callbackFlow` is how a legacy listener API, such as a fraud engine's event callbacks or a JMS listener, becomes a Flow with clean unregistering. For a Kafka consumer, keep offset commits in order: a fan-out pool processes records out of order, so commit only what every worker has finished, or keep one worker per partition.
mistake: The most common mistake is a channel that nobody closes, or a `callbackFlow` without `awaitClose`. In the first case the receiving `for` loop never ends, so the `coroutineScope` around it never returns, and the request hangs with no error and no CPU use. In the second, `callbackFlow` throws `IllegalStateException` the first time it is collected, and the fix people reach for, an `awaitCancellation()` or a `delay(Long.MAX_VALUE)`, keeps the flow open but never unregisters the listener. Use `produce { }`, which closes its channel when the block ends; close fan-in channels after `joinAll()`; and end every `callbackFlow` with `awaitClose { unregister() }`.

compare.title: A capped worker pool: ExecutorService vs channel and coroutines

java.title: RefundRunner.java

kotlin.title: RefundRunner.kt

compare.note: Both cap the issuer at 8 concurrent refunds and collect results in the order they finish. The Java version spends 8 threads, which sit blocked while the issuer thinks, and it queues every task up front. The Kotlin version spends 8 coroutines, which suspend while waiting, and the rendezvous channel hands out ids only as workers free up, so a list of a million ids never sits in a task queue. The bigger difference is failure. In Java one failed refund shows up at `get()`, and the other tasks keep running until `close()` waits for them. In Kotlin the whole pipeline is one `coroutineScope`, so the first failure cancels the producer and every worker before the exception reaches the caller.

steps.say: An acquirer's settlement file has 200,000 lines. Each line must be parsed, enriched with a BIN lookup (a blocking legacy client, 20 ms per call), and posted to the ledger in batches of 500. Doing it in one loop takes over an hour, almost all of it in BIN lookups.
Stage 1 reads and parses on IO, into a small buffer. `produce` closes the channel when the file ends.
Stage 2 fans out to 16 enrichers, the BIN service's limit. They fan in to one channel, closed when all 16 are done.

Stage 3 is a single writer, so ledger batches stay simple. When `postings` is closed and drained, the loop ends, and `coroutineScope` returns once every stage has finished. If any stage throws, the scope cancels the others.

Self-check: the ledger slows to a crawl. Trace what happens to memory and to the BIN service. (The writer falls behind, `postings` fills up to 1,000, the enrichers suspend in `send`, `records` fills up to 100, and the parser suspends too. Memory stays flat, and the BIN service sees fewer calls. Backpressure flows all the way back to the file read.)

lab.title: A worker pool, an event bridge and a hedged quote
steps: Run the tests. Five of seven fail. `PipelineModel.kt` has the bus, its `Registration` and `Quote`.

In `ParallelSettlement.kt`, build the pool inside `coroutineScope`: `produce` the ids, start `workers` coroutines that loop over the ids channel and send `id to settle(id)` into a receipts channel, close receipts after `joinAll()`, and read it into a map.
In `EventBusFlow.kt`, keep the `Registration` that `register` returns, and end the block with `awaitClose { registration.unregister() }`.
In `FastestQuote.kt`, start every call with `async`, `select` on their `onAwait` clauses, cancel all the calls, and return the winner.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: `produce` needs `@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)` on the function. It closes its channel when its block ends.
Close the receipts channel from its own coroutine: `launch { pool.joinAll(); receipts.close() }`. If you close it after the receiving loop, the loop never ends.
`awaitClose` comes from `kotlinx.coroutines.channels`. It suspends until the collector stops, so it must be the last line of the `callbackFlow` block.
`select { calls.forEach { c -> c.onAwait { it } } }` is a whole `select`: the lambda registers one clause per call. Cancelling a call that already finished does nothing, so you can cancel them all.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: A `Channel` hands each element to exactly one receiver. `send` and `receive` suspend instead of blocking.
Capacity sets the pace: rendezvous (the default) hands over directly, `Channel(n)` buffers n, `UNLIMITED` never suspends (and can run out of memory), `CONFLATED` keeps only the newest.
Close a channel when sending is done, or `for (x in channel)` never ends. `produce { }` closes its channel for you.
Fan-out (several workers on one channel) caps concurrency at the number of workers. Fan-in channels close after `joinAll()`. Inside `coroutineScope`, one failure cancels the whole pipeline.
`select` takes whichever clause completes first (`onAwait`, `onReceive`, `onTimeout`). It is biased to the first clause, and stopping the losers is your job.
`callbackFlow` bridges listener APIs and must end with `awaitClose { unregister() }`. `buffer`, `conflate` and `collectLatest` trade completeness for speed or freshness.

quiz.q: `val ch = Channel<String>()`. A coroutine runs `ch.send("batch-1"); println("sent")`, and nothing ever receives from `ch`. What happens?
options: `sent` prints at once, because `send` puts the element in a buffer
`send` suspends forever, so `sent` never prints
`send` throws `IllegalStateException` because nobody is receiving
The element is dropped and `sent` prints
quiz.why: The default capacity is rendezvous: `send` waits until a receiver takes the element. With no receiver it waits forever, and the coroutine never finishes. A buffered channel would accept it at once.

quiz.q: Four workers each run `for (id in ids) settle(id)` on the same channel. The producer sends 40 ids and closes it. Which statement is true?
options: Each id is settled exactly once, and at most 4 settle calls run at the same time
Each id is settled four times, once per worker
All 40 go to the first worker, because it started first
The workers deadlock, because they compete for the same channel
quiz.why: A channel is a queue: each element goes to one receiver, and fair receiving spreads the ids across the waiting workers. Four workers means at most four calls in flight. That is fan-out.

options: Events flow normally until the collector cancels
Nothing is ever emitted, but the collector waits forever
`callbackFlow` throws `IllegalStateException`, because the block returned without `awaitClose`
The listener is unregistered automatically when the block returns
quiz.why: `callbackFlow` requires the block to suspend in `awaitClose { }` until the collector stops. If the block returns while the channel is still open, it throws `IllegalStateException`, and the listener it registered is never unregistered.

quiz.q: A pricing service recomputes a merchant's FX quote every time the amount in the checkout changes. A recompute takes 300 ms, and amounts change every 100 ms while the customer types. Only the latest quote matters, and a stale computation should stop. Which operator fits?
options: `buffer()`
`conflate()`
`Channel.UNLIMITED` between input and pricing
`collectLatest { }`
quiz.why: `collectLatest` cancels the computation in progress when a new amount arrives, so only the latest is computed to the end. `conflate` skips values that arrive while busy but still finishes every computation it starts. `buffer` and an unlimited channel compute every stale amount.

quiz.q: From the reactive track: which Kotlin Flow operator behaves most like Reactor's `onBackpressureLatest()`?
options: `buffer()`
`conflate()`
`collectLatest { }`
`flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)`
quiz.why: Both keep only the newest value while the consumer is busy and hand it over when the consumer is ready. `collectLatest` is closer to `switchMap`, because it cancels the work in progress. `buffer` is `onBackpressureBuffer`.

flashcards.front: What is the default capacity of `Channel<T>()`, and what does it mean for `send`?
flashcards.back: `RENDEZVOUS` (0): `send` suspends until a receiver takes the element.

flashcards.front: What does a `Channel.CONFLATED` channel do with a new element when one is already waiting?
flashcards.back: It replaces the waiting one. `send` never suspends, and a slow receiver gets only the newest.

flashcards.front: Several coroutines receive from one channel. How many of them get each element?
flashcards.back: Exactly one. That is fan-out, and it caps concurrency at the number of receivers.
When the channel has been closed and every element in it has been received.

flashcards.front: Why must a `callbackFlow` block end with `awaitClose { ... }`?
flashcards.back: It keeps the flow open until the collector stops, then runs the cleanup. Without it, `callbackFlow` throws `IllegalStateException` and the listener leaks.

flashcards.front: Two `select` clauses are ready at the same moment. Which one wins?
flashcards.back: The one listed first: `select` is biased toward the first clause.
`conflate` skips values that arrived while busy but finishes each one it starts. `collectLatest` cancels the block in progress when a new value arrives.

terms.plain: A queue between coroutines: each element is received once, and send and receive suspend instead of blocking.
A channel with no buffer: the sender waits until a receiver takes the element.
Several receivers on one channel, so each element is handled by exactly one of them.
Several senders into one channel, read by one receiver.
A builder that starts a coroutine sending into a new channel and closes it when the block ends.
Waits for whichever of several clauses can complete first, and runs only that one.
A flow builder with a channel inside, for turning listener callbacks into a Flow.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to settle 50,000 batches with `batchIds.map { async { settle(it) } }.awaitAll()`, and the acquirer allows 8 concurrent calls. Explain the problem and how a channel-based worker pool fixes it.
explain_back.answer: That code starts 50,000 coroutines at once, so the acquirer sees 50,000 concurrent calls, far more than its limit of 8. We'd get rate-limited or time out, and we'd hold 50,000 pending requests in memory. With a channel, one producer sends the ids into a rendezvous channel and 8 worker coroutines loop over it. Each id goes to exactly one worker, so at most 8 settle calls are in flight, and the producer just waits until a worker is free, which keeps memory flat. The workers send their receipts into a second channel that one loop reads, and a separate coroutine closes it after all the workers finish so that loop can end. Because it all runs inside coroutineScope, one failed settle cancels the producer and the other workers and the exception reaches the caller.

deeper.body:
`actor { }`, which older tutorials use to protect shared state with a channel of messages, is marked `@ObsoleteCoroutinesApi`: the KDoc says it will become obsolete when "complex actors" arrive. A plain coroutine looping over a channel you create does the same job without the warning. `BroadcastChannel` was deprecated in 1.7, and its deprecation level was raised in 1.9. Use `SharedFlow` (lesson 8 of this track) for one-to-many.

The `BUFFERED` default of 64 comes from the JVM system property `kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer`. It is also the buffer `flowOn`, `buffer()`, `channelFlow` and `callbackFlow` use unless you pass a size. When you size a pipeline for memory, count those hidden buffers too.

Channels also have `trySend` and `tryReceive`, which never suspend and return a `ChannelResult`. They are for code at the edge that can't suspend, like a listener callback, and `trySendBlocking` is the blocking variant for a plain thread that may wait. Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.11, `ReceiveChannel.consumeTo(collection)` drains a channel into a collection.

The prime-sieve pipeline in the official channels guide is a fun read: each prime gets its own filtering coroutine, chained by channels, so the pipeline grows as it runs. It is a good picture of how cheap coroutines and channels are, and a poor model for production code, where a fixed number of stages with a known number of workers is far easier to monitor and to cancel.
